utterances.text: I was assigned to the conference for almost exactly one year, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from mid-December, 1992 until the 1st of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify who the Bosnian Serb negotiators were at that conference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The Serb delegation varied over time. For most of the negotiations, only a small party were present, but they were led by Dr. Karadzic, but also in attendance on occasions was General Mladic, but not frequently. Mr. Krajisnik was frequently there. I have -- I don't recall the frequency with which Mrs. Plavsic or Mr. Koljevic may or may not have attended. They -- they were the principal officers representing the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet with Mr. Krajisnik or to observe Mr. Krajisnik during the course of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I would say that I never really met with Mr. Krajisnik, but I was present in the room with him on many occasions. I was able to observe the negotiations. Usually I did not sit at the table but sat at a chair behind, and I was able to observe and take notes on what was happening during those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, as part of your advice capacity and part of your observations, did you take the measure of the various negotiators?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did. That was one of the responsibilities of those observers, that you were to take notes to make sure that at the end of the day when reports had to be written up that all matters were covered, and part of that debriefing process was the participation of the various negotiators and an assessment of what their role was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the role of Mr. Krajisnik as you observed it and as you assessed it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik did not have a lot to say, I assume this is because he didn't speak English. But certainly he was very carefully consulted by Mr. Karadzic or Dr. Karadzic. He sat at a central part of the table, and he seemed to be a very important member of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout these negotiations, either formally or in informal conversations, did the Bosnian Serbs set forth their positions in respect of their territorial ambitions, their territorial objectives and their views toward non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They clearly stated their position and in great detail. When it came to negotiating over the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina and how the territory might be divided up into different ethnic identities there was a great deal of argument, supporting argument, for the division, and there was a continual restatement of the Serb concerns for their safety of their people, the need for a republic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say in respect of living -- the ability to live with non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, at various times, they indicated that it was no longer possible for the three nations to continue to live together in harmony in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was necessary to physically and politically separate the nations, otherwise the Serb people would continue to live under threat, and that this was no longer a viable solution for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a uniform Serb position that was taken by the negotiators on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was repeatedly stated at many, many meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the -- these negotiations, who were the main negotiators for the international community?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: This depended upon the topic, but certainly Mr. Cyrus Vance initially in the period December to -- of 1992 until approximately May of 1993, he really led the negotiations on behalf of the international community. And then in the period after May 1993, Lord Owen really was the intellectual leader of the -- the conference. Mr. Stoltenberg, when he arrived, played more of a support role to Lord Owen, but there were also a number of ambassadors attached to the conference who led individual negotiations on smaller topics. But on the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was generally the co-chairman who led the discussions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At these negotiations, were the Bosnian Serb leaders confronted with accusations of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At these negotiations, were the Bosnian Serbs confronted by claims -- confronted by the co-chairman or by others who were conducting the negotiations about claims of ethnic cleansing committed by the Serbs in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they were. This was a -- my understanding is this was a frequent topic. Lord Owen, on occasions when negotiations were not progressing smoothly, would sometimes lecture the participants on their conduct and on their -- on their conduct and their failure to respect human -- human rights. He was very forthright in this regard. It was like an irritated headmaster talking to an errant schoolboy and there was not much diplomacy involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, he was blunt and direct; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serbs have at their disposal interpreters when these -- when Lord Owen and others made such accusations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they did. During central forums interpreters were usually provided by the United Nations; however, in the more common smaller working groups, the parties usually brought their own interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that -- oh, sorry. Did it appear to you that the Bosnian Serbs understood Lord Owen when he was making those accusations and understood the accusations made by others about ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic understood English very well and Lord Owen's address was made in English, or certainly made in the presence of all of the Serb delegation. Whether it was translated for them into Serbian Croat, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of Dr. Karadzic to such claims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Usually a -- a restatement of the need to defend the Serb people, the need for a Serb republic. The circumstances were actually quite embarrassing for Dr. Karadzic, and I guess his delegation, because Lord Owen was very direct in what he said and used very blunt language, so there was an air of embarrassment. But essentially, the Serb party responded by restating their position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- maybe you can help the Trial Chamber understand this. How was it or when did -- actually let me withdraw that. The discussions that took place at the conference involved discussions about territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was one of the issues. The other significant one was a constitution that the new political entity could use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us focus on the questions of the territory. Can you just inform the Court, when certain parts of the territory were under discussion did the issue arise about ethnic cleansing in the context of those discussions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what you mean by that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Could you restate it or rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there certain boundary lines that were established that were under discussion in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: About 80, 85 per cent of the division was broadly agreed by the three parties as being an acceptable solution, if there needed to be a division. The argument was really about 10 or 15 per cent. And the discussions were done in considerable detail with the benefit of the various census that had been done by the former Yugoslavia -- the government of the former Yugoslavia in that area. There were quite detailed arguments about historical claims to quite small geographic areas. When the co-chairman would indicate that an area which was claimed by -- by one party might contain a significant minority from another nation or group, all three parties seemed quite comfortable with the idea of relocating large numbers of people from those contested areas. There was never any really denial of facts on the ground that areas had -- no longer had their original population, that there had been already in the process of the war ethnic cleansing or relocation of population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stayed in those negotiations through December of 1993; is that correct, General Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on your contacts with Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, based on information at your disposal, did you form an opinion as to the hierarchical relationship amongst the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your conclusions in respect of that leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were the principal political power or authority within that grouping. Though while Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic may well have had some political authority, on the real issues, the important issues, was Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic who had the significant say. I think General Mladic probably had significant input too on a -- not only on the military side, but perhaps in influencing political outcomes. The short answer, I think, the political leadership was dominated by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Wilson. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Stewart, is it -- I am informed that if you now start your cross-examination, that we might finish tomorrow for a considerable time, not having any further witnesses. Mr. Harmon, is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- Your Honour, I had trouble hearing you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that your next witness would not be available until Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there's no specific need at this moment to start your cross-examination, Mr. Stewart, where usually the Chamber insists on continuing, there might be less reason to do so at this very moment. Therefore, my question to you is whether you'd like to start your cross- examination now or whether you'd prefer to start it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I -- Your Honour, I think it's the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the -- the answer with that adjustment, the answer to Your Honour's question is I would prefer to start it tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Wilson, you may have noticed that I address you as Mr. Wilson and not as General Wilson as many do. That's merely an expression of whatever witness here, in whatever capacity he works outside, is here to testify -- to assist the Chamber to find the truth and that it's -- it's not any disrespect of your position. You've heard that the Defence would prefer to start to cross- examining you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants the request of the Defence. That means that we'd like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you still are about to give. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Wilson out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have some time left but we also have some time left tomorrow, I'd like to address two matters at this moment and a few other procedural matters tomorrow. Since I take it, Mr. Stewart, that you would not need the whole morning for -- the whole afternoon for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like to bring to the attention of the parties has to do with the procedure for examining expert witnesses. This Chamber is not inclined to set a new Guinness Book of Records standard for who goes quickest through the most documents in one hour. The experience this Chamber has gained with 18 binders in three days or 12 binders in one day and a half does not encourage the Chamber to proceed in the same way in this respect. Therefore, I'd like to give some guidance on the procedure for examining expert witnesses. I'll do it by giving you six points. If the parties, who have not been consulted on these points, would like to briefly respond tomorrow when we have some time available for procedural matters, they will be allowed to do so. Point 1: Following affirmation of the witness as an expert witness, the central item of evidence is the expert's report. 2: The Prosecution is instructed to limit its examination to matters of central importance to the case which are likely to be controversial and which require further explanation, clarification, or illustration in terms of how the opinion was arrived at by the expert. 3: Limit on exhibits by the Prosecution. The Prosecution is invited to tender documents referred to in the expert report which are necessary to achieve the purpose of point 2 and, in re-examination, to deal with matters raised in cross-examination. 4: Use of exhibits by the Defence. The Defence may introduce into evidence, in addition to any of its own documents, any supporting documents referred to in the expert report which have not yet been admitted and on which the Defence relies in cross-examination. 5. All remaining documentation underlying the expert report will not be admitted into evidence unless one of the parties, showing good cause in light of the above, or the Chamber itself, specifically requests so. 6. In relation to point 5, the parties are referred to the Chamber's guidance to the parties delivered orally on the 1st of March of this year and on the 27th April 2005, the transcript references being transcript page 9606 and for the 27th of April, 12754. Then the next issue is, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber owes you a response to a request made in relation to the scheduling of 98 bis matters. The Chamber recalls that at a recent housekeeping session on the 27th of April of this year you, Mr. Stewart, expressed your concern that the date set by the April scheduling order for the Defence's Rule 98 bis submissions comes too close to the tail end of the summer recess. Mr. Stewart, you suggested that much, if not all, of the summer recess would therefore have to be given over to preparations for 98 bis submissions and that members of the Defence team would all -- would as a result have little or no time to take vacation. Mr. Stewart, you requested the Chamber to comment on this concern, and I promised you that we would do so. The scheduling order of the 26th of April, 2005 has the Prosecution's case closing on or before the 22nd of July, 2005. At this stage, we don't know when the Prosecution's case will actually close, so to that extent, Mr. Stewart, your application is somewhat premature, but I'm going to assume for argument's sake that the Prosecution's case does close on the 22nd of July, as scheduled. There are 16 working days in the period after the 22nd of July and before the 16th of August. The 16th of August is the day reserved for oral submissions on the acquittal motion, assuming that there is one. The Chamber was never under the impression that the Defence team would spend all 16 work days of the summer recess working on their 98 bis submissions. This is because the 98 bis procedure, as it was amended last year, is not the work-intensive milestone it once used to be. The Rule was amended precisely with the aim of keeping the milestone in place while reducing the workload that had come to be associated with it. The Chamber is not expecting, and indeed will not accept, any written submissions on the 98 bis motion. The Defence is simply to notify the Chamber and the Prosecution at the close of the Prosecution's case whether it intends to move for acquittal. This may be done orally, or by e-mail, and no reasons need to be given at that stage. If the Defence notifies the Chamber of its intention to move for acquittal, it will be invited to do so orally on the 16th of August. There will be an opportunity for an oral response from the Prosecution. The Chamber will then decide the matter, again orally, within three days. The new oral format of the 98 bis procedure changes the nature of the preparation required, while not in any way diminishing the Chamber's responsibility to make a considered decision. If the Defence intends to move for acquittal, it should begin already now to develop the points it wishes to make come the 16th of August. There is no reason to wait for the Prosecution's last witness to be heard before such an exercise may start. Indeed, by the time of the last Prosecution witness, the Defence should be aiming to be finalising any 98 bis submissions it intends to make. The same is true also of the Prosecution, which under the new procedure is effectively obliged to anticipate the Defence arguments and respond to them within a very short time frame. In the present case, the Prosecution must be prepared to respond to the Defence on the very same day it hears the Defence's submissions. I think it is clear, therefore, that the amended 98 bis procedure obliges both parties and, for that matter, the Chamber, to think about the midpoint review well in advance of the date of the review. On the understanding that the 98 bis procedure cannot be a last- minute exercise, it follows in the Chamber's mind that the 98 bis dates which have been set by the scheduling order are reasonable. This, Mr. Stewart, concludes my remarks on your observation or application for an answer. We will adjourn until tomorrow in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom and expect you then to start cross-examination, Mr. Stewart. We'll adjourn.
